statement: In family members (mostly women: spouses, partners and parents) of adults with alcohol or other drug problems who refused treatment, training the family member in CRAFT (community reinforcement and family training; in the largest trial about 12 hours of individual sessions with a therapist, teaching ways to reward not drinking, to communicate, to handle dangerous situations and to suggest treatment) compared with twelve-step family approaches increases the share of relatives who enter treatment, in four small US randomized trials published 1986–2002, three of them from the groups that developed CRAFT and its first version. In the largest trial (130 family members in Albuquerque, USA, 91% women, living with a relative with a drinking problem and seeing them on at least 40% of days; Miller et al., 1999), the relative entered treatment within 6 months (at least an assessment and one session) in 29 of 45 cases (64 in 100) after CRAFT, 12 of 40 (30 in 100) after a Johnson Institute intervention, which prepares the family for a group confrontation, and 6 of 45 (13 in 100) after Al-Anon facilitation, up to 12 individual sessions encouraging involvement in Al-Anon, which the authors note is not the same as a simple referral to Al-Anon; in the Johnson group, 70 in 100 families chose not to hold the confrontation, and 9 of the 12 that did saw their relative enter treatment. Across the four trials (two on alcohol, two on illicit drugs, cocaine most often), relatives entered treatment in 84 of 125 CRAFT cases (67 in 100) against 18 of 99 with Al-Anon or Nar-Anon approaches (18 in 100): relative risk 3.25 (95% CI 2.11 to 5.02), with every trial pointing the same way (I² 2.9%; Roozen et al., 2010); the comparison with the Johnson intervention rests on the one trial (relative risk 2.15, 1.28 to 3.62), which the review's discussion calls almost three times as effective. Family members' own depression, anger and family relationships improved over 6 months by similar amounts in all three groups of the largest trial, whether or not the relative entered treatment; with no group left without help, no approach can be credited with that improvement, and the review's pooled 'improvement' compares scores before and after within the CRAFT groups only. The trials counted whether the relative started treatment, not drinking or drug use, which the largest trial reports separately (not read here), or safety; relatives with recent violence, injecting or crack cocaine use were excluded from the largest trial; family members and therapists knew which approach they had; therapists were not crossed with approaches (in the largest trial, CRAFT's less experienced therapists were supervised by the approach's developer, a co-author); and the review is rated critically low on AMSTAR 2 on its study card (no protocol, no list of excluded studies, no trial-by-trial risk-of-bias judgments, no check for unpublished trials). Certainty: moderate, for treatment entry against twelve-step family approaches. Status: replicated.
plain: Can family members help get someone who refuses treatment into it? A skills course for families called CRAFT did better than the other approaches tested. In the biggest trial, with 130 family members of people with drinking problems, 64 in 100 relatives started treatment within 6 months after CRAFT, against 30 in 100 after training for a family confrontation (7 in 10 of those families decided not to hold it) and 13 in 100 after counselling aimed at joining Al-Anon. Across four small US trials, two about alcohol and two about other drugs, relatives started treatment about 3 times as often with CRAFT as with Al-Anon or Nar-Anon approaches (67 against 18 in 100). Family members' own mood and family life improved in every group, whether or not their relative started treatment, but with no group left without help, no approach can take the credit. Three of the four trials came from the teams behind CRAFT, the trials counted only whether treatment started, not whether drinking or drug use changed, and families living with violence were left out of the biggest trial.
population: Family members (spouses, partners, parents and other relatives; 88–100% women across trials; aged 19 to 81) of adults with alcohol problems (two trials) or illicit drug use, cocaine most often (two trials), who refused treatment, in four US randomized trials published 1986–2002 (264 family members). In the largest trial, 130 family members in Albuquerque, New Mexico (91% women; 59% spouses, 30% parents; recruited mostly through local news media), living with the relative and seeing them on at least 40% of days; relatives with recent violence, injecting or crack cocaine use, or a more severe illicit drug problem were excluded
exposure: CRAFT (community reinforcement and family training): in the largest trial up to 12 one-hour individual sessions (about 12 hours of therapist contact) teaching the family member to reward not drinking, communicate positively, plan competing activities, handle dangerous situations and suggest treatment; in the oldest trial its first version, community reinforcement training
comparator: Twelve-step family approaches (Al-Anon facilitation therapy, an Al-Anon model or Nar-Anon) in all four trials; a Johnson Institute intervention, which prepares family members for a group confrontation, in one trial; no untreated group in any trial
outcome: The relative entering treatment (at least one session; in the largest trial an assessment and at least one session within 6 months); family members' own depression, anger, family cohesion and conflict, and relationship happiness
magnitude: Miller et al. (1999), engaged within 6 months: CRAFT 29/45 (64%), Johnson 12/40 (30%), Al-Anon facilitation 6/45 (13%); χ²(2, N = 130) = 27.33, p < .0001; CRAFT against Johnson χ²(1, N = 85) = 10.29, p < .001; Al-Anon facilitation against Johnson p < .06. Editors' calculation (Wald 95% intervals): CRAFT minus Johnson 34.4 percentage points (14.5 to 54.4); CRAFT minus Al-Anon facilitation 51.1 points (34.0 to 68.3). Within 12 months 67%, 35% and 20% (Table 1). Adjusted for drinking at intake, extra therapy and relationship type: Wald χ²(2, N = 120) = 17.27, p < .0002. Johnson group: 70% did not hold the confrontation; 9 of the 12 that did saw the relative enter treatment, against 3 of 28 within 6 months. Across groups, parents engaged the relative more often than spouses (51% against 32% at 6 months). Family members: no group-by-time interaction and no group effect; Beck Depression Inventory means 10.6–10.8 at intake and 7.0–7.5 at 6 months in all three groups. Roozen et al. (2010): CRAFT against Al-Anon/Nar-Anon, 4 trials, 84/125 (67%) against 18/99 (18%), RR 3.25 (95% CI 2.11–5.02), NNT 2, I² 2.9%; trial RRs 9.75 (0.67–141.44), 4.83 (2.22–10.50), 3.86 (1.28–11.64), 2.34 (1.31–4.16); without the smallest trial 3.21 (1.99–5.17); CRAFT against Johnson (one trial) RR 2.15 (1.28–3.62), NNT 3; within CRAFT groups, baseline against 6 months, depression WMD 3.60 (0.99–6.22), 74 family members in two trials.

evidence.extracted: Urn randomization balancing seven characteristics. Al-Anon facilitation: up to 12 sessions of 60 minutes, adapted from Project MATCH. Johnson Institute intervention: six sessions of about 2 hours, preparing the family to confront the drinker. CRAFT replicated and extended the approach tested by Sisson and Azrin (1986), originally developed by Robert J. Meyers (second author), who supervised this condition: awareness training, rewarding not drinking, communication skills, competing and outside activities, handling dangerous situations and suggesting counselling, all in individual sessions. All approaches manual-guided with about 12 hours of contact; therapists nested within approaches; CRAFT's five therapists had less experience (four with 0–3 years) than those in the other approaches.

risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_miller_1999 (RoB 2): some concerns (allocation concealment not described; no registered plan). Beyond those questions: family members and therapists knew the assignment; therapists were nested within approaches, with CRAFT's less experienced therapists supervised by its developer, a co-author, and the two main CRAFT therapists engaged 50% and 91% of their cases; three of the four pooled trials come from the groups that developed CRAFT and its first version, and the review (card sc_roozen_2010: AMSTAR 2 critically low) reports only a summary quality score for each trial. Entry into treatment was largely recorded by the projects rather than rated by the family members. One level, not two: the difference is large, and every trial, including the one with no author in common with the others (Kirby et al., 1999, as summarized by the review), points the same way.

inconsistency.note: I² 2.9%; all four trial estimates favour CRAFT (relative risks 2.34 to 9.75).

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: treatment entry, the outcome measured, in families of adults who refused treatment, in US trials with trained and supervised therapists delivering about 12 hours of sessions. The statement says that drinking and drug use, safety, families living with violence and family members in less frequent contact are outside it.

imprecision.note: 224 family members and 102 treatment entries in the pooled comparison; the interval (2.11 to 5.02) excludes small effects. The comparison with the Johnson intervention (one trial of 85; 1.28 to 3.62) is less precise and is worded as resting on one trial.

publication_bias.note: Not investigated by the review, and with four trials no test would be informative; the search left out trial registries and grey literature. The concern that small trials from the developers' groups dominate is counted under risk of bias, not twice.

grade.reasoning: Randomized trials start high (METHODS 6.3); risk of bias −1 (see the domain note), which gives moderate, for the statement that training family members in CRAFT, rather than in a twelve-step family approach, increases the share of relatives who enter treatment. Causal wording ('increases') fits the randomized design at this certainty. The comparison with the Johnson intervention rests on one trial and is worded as such; on its own it would be rated lower for imprecision. The statements about family members' own wellbeing describe what the trials found (no difference between approaches, improvement in all groups) and are not rated as an effect of any approach, since no trial had an untreated group; the review's within-group pooling cannot answer that question. The claim does not adopt the review's 'almost three times' for the Johnson comparison (its own result is a relative risk of 2.15), its suggestion that partner violence may also have fallen (no data, and the largest trial excluded families with recent violence), or its 'strong evidence' that the approaches improve family members' functioning. Status replicated: four trials point the same way, one of them from a team with no author in common with the developers' trials; two of the four share authors.
